name: Femi Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a response team out of the Harbour Street station, right in the old docks part of the city where the warehouses got turned into flats. A shift is calls, calls, calls: a shoplifter at the big supermarket, a neighbour dispute over a parked van, a man in crisis on the canal bridge. In between I'm in the car with my crewmate Dana typing up statements on the tablet. I love the bridge calls, honestly, when you talk someone back and they shake your hand after. What wears me out is the paperwork, which can be half my shift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Half your shift on paperwork? How do you handle that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cheat a bit, in a legal way. I use an AI app on my own phone to tidy my rough notes into proper sentences before I type them into the force system, never with names or anything private in it. It saves me maybe forty minutes a night. Some of the older lads think it's lazy, but I'd rather be out on the street than stuck at a keyboard in the report room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the tools are useful but they're not magic. At work I'd tell people to try them for the boring stuff and stop being scared of them. Online I'd probably post something like, see, the robots aren't coming for the cops, they're just doing our typing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's fine for me, maybe slightly boring. I've got my savings, about eight months of pay sitting there, and policing isn't going anywhere in this picture. The real problems stay the same ones we've got now, like not enough mental health services, so we end up being the ambulance and the social worker at 3am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and keep pushing the force to approve a proper report tool so people don't use their own phones. I'd apply for the sergeant's exam next year like I planned. And I'd keep pushing with the union on staffing for the night shift, because that's the thing that actually hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed, to be honest. A bit flat, because I'm someone who likes new things. But no worries about my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the real problem is being the ambulance and the social worker. Tell me about a night like that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month we spent six hours in A&E with a young woman who'd been sectioned, because there was no mental health bed in the whole city. Six hours, two officers, while calls stacked up on the screen. No AI fixes that. That's a funding problem, and I'd say that to anyone at City Hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what would you push the union for, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More officers on nights and a proper mental health team that we can call instead of doing it ourselves. I'm the union rep for our team, so I'd take it to the branch meeting. Boring AI or not, that fight is the same.

say: The AI tools are **handy for typing**, but they don't change what policing is.
The real fight is **staffing and mental health** services, not technology.
think: My **job is safe** and my savings cover eight months, so this picture changes little for me.
The force still wastes officers on **six-hour hospital waits** that no app will fix.
do: Push the force to approve an **official report tool** so officers stop using their own phones.
Sit the **sergeant's exam** next year as already planned.
Raise **night-shift staffing** at the union branch meeting.
feel: **Relaxed** about the job, and a little **bored** by how little changes.
S0.quote: Last month we spent six hours in A&E with a young woman who'd been sectioned, because there was no mental health bed in the whole city.
fieldNote: He talks about AI as a **typing helper** and moves straight on to staffing.
His real anger is at **underfunded services** that turn officers into carers.
As union rep, he frames everything as a **collective fight** rather than a personal one.

steps.text: Push for an approved AI report tool for the whole team
Sit the sergeant's exam next spring
Raise night-shift staffing at the next union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news if we do it right. If AI takes the statements, the case files and the call logging, officers get back on the street. Online I'd say the public should be asking who owns the software and who checks it, because that's where it can go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. Maybe a third of my day is writing and checking, and I'm the guy who already uses the tools. The risk is the force using it as an excuse to cut call handlers and the back office, and I'd hate that for people like Marcia in our control room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for any pilot straight away, the first month it's offered. I'd do one of those online courses on AI and evidence, so I understand where it messes up, maybe three hundred in fees out of my own pocket. And I'd get the union to write rules about it before management does: no AI deciding who gets stopped, and no job cuts sneaked in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. There's a small knot about the control room staff. But I feel like this is my moment, a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Marcia in the control room. What would you say to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My control room colleague Marcia has been answering 999 calls for twenty years, and an AI on the non-urgent line is the first thing a budget officer will want. She's brilliant at calming people. I'd tell her the union will fight for her role, and I'd mean it, but privately I'd be scared for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a role you'd want for yourself in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There'd be a new team checking the AI's work, making sure the case files are right before they go to the prosecutors. I'd want to be on that. It's still police work, it's just a different kind of careful.

say: AI doing **statements and case files** would get officers back on the street.
The public should ask **who owns the software** and who checks it.
think: About a **third of my day** is writing and checking, so this mostly frees me up.
The danger is the force using it to **cut control room** staff like Marcia (a call handler).
do: Volunteer for the **first AI pilot** the force offers.
Pay about **300 for a course** on AI and evidence.
Get the union to set **rules on AI** before management does.
feel: Mostly **excited**, as if this is his moment.
A small **knot of worry** for the control room staff.
S1.quote: My control room colleague Marcia has been answering 999 calls for twenty years, and an AI on the non-urgent line is the first thing a budget officer will want.
fieldNote: He sees the change as **good for himself** and immediately worries about others.
His union instinct is to **write rules first**, before managers set them.
He already has a **target role**: checking AI-made case files.

steps.text: Volunteer for the force's first AI case-file pilot
Pay for an online course on AI and evidence
Ask the union to draft AI rules before management

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and get rules in place, fast. At work I'd say policing has to stay human, because you can't have a machine deciding to arrest someone. Online I'd be one of the loud ones saying the government has to step in for everyone losing their jobs, not just us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's scarier than I'd admit. The thinking half of my job, the reports, the risk checks, even deciding which call to go to first, all of that goes in 2028. Then in 2031 there are robots that can stand on a bridge and do my hands-on half. I'm 27, so I'd be 32 with a job that might be half gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd stop thinking about sergeant and start thinking about what can't be handed over. I'd go for the crisis negotiation course, because talking people down is the thing I'm best at and the hardest to hand to a machine. I'd keep my savings untouched and add to them. And I'd push the union and the federation to get a deal on retraining before the robots come in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit sick. I like being early on tech, but this is too early for everyone. My stomach drops when I think of three years with only half a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'half a job'. What does that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Picture me riding along while a system tells me where to go and writes everything up. I'm basically the hands and the face for three years. Then the hands go too. Maybe what's left is a few of us doing the talking and the arrests nobody wants a robot doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Amara is a paramedic, so we'd be in the same boat, sort of. I'd tell Amara we're fine for money for a long time, but that I don't know what I'll be doing at thirty. And I'd say we should not buy the flat we were looking at until we know.

say: Policing must **stay human**, because a machine shouldn't decide on arrests.
The government has to **step in** for everyone losing work, not just police.
think: The **thinking half** of his job goes in 2028, and the **hands-on half** by 2031.
He'd be **32** with **half a job**, and that frightens him more than he'd admit.
do: Apply for the **crisis negotiation course** in the first month.
Leave his **eight months of savings** untouched and keep adding.
Push the union for a **retraining deal** before 2031.
feel: A bit **sick**, despite liking new technology.
His **stomach drops** at three years with only half a job.
S2.quote: I'm 27, so I'd be 32 with a job that might be half gone.
fieldNote: The early adopter turns **cautious** once the speed is this fast.
He bets on **crisis talking** as the human skill that lasts.
He'd **delay buying a flat** with his partner, a sign the worry is real.

steps.text: Apply for the force's crisis negotiation course
Hold off buying the flat with Amara until things settle
Keep adding to the eight months of savings
Push the union for a retraining deal before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but calmer: we have five years, so let's use them properly. At work I'd say every officer should get trained on these systems now, not after. Online I'd argue for a law that says arrests and use of force stay with humans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years changes it for me. I'd be 32 when the thinking AI lands and 35 when the robots come, and by then I could be in a role that's hard to replace. It's still fast, but it's enough time to get ahead of it instead of being dragged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd do the negotiation course and then try for a spot in the force's new tech and standards unit, the one that checks how systems are used. I'd start a part-time degree in criminology, two evenings a week, which the force half pays for. And I'd take the union work further, maybe stand for the branch committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but in a way I can use. It feels like a race I could actually win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the standards unit and not something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because somebody has to stand between the machine and the public and say, no, that stop wasn't fair. I've seen what happens when a new system goes wrong, like the number plate cameras that flagged the wrong cars for a month. I want to be the one who catches that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've put a lot on the union. What if the union can't stop it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then at least we'd have a say in how it goes. I'm not naive, the union didn't stop the station closures either. But a seat at the table means retraining money and not just a letter saying thanks for your service.

say: Every officer should be **trained on AI** now, not after it arrives.
A law should keep **arrests and force** with humans.
think: Five years means he's **35 when robots** come and could be somewhere safer by then.
It feels like **enough time** to get ahead rather than be dragged.
do: Take the **negotiation course**, then apply to the **standards unit**.
Start a **part-time criminology degree**, half paid by the force.
feel: **Nervous**, but in a way he can use.
It feels like a **race he could win**.
S3.quote: Somebody has to stand between the machine and the public and say, no, that stop wasn't fair.
fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into a **career plan** almost instantly.
He wants to **police the machines**, not compete with them.
He's honest that the union **lost before**, over station closures.

steps.text: Apply to the force's tech and standards unit
Start a part-time criminology degree, two evenings a week
Stand for the union branch committee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so no excuses. At work I'd tell the younger ones to plan their careers around it. Online I'd keep pushing for the same rules: humans make the big calls, and nobody gets thrown away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years suits me fine. I'd be 37 when AGI hits and 40 when the robots come, and I'd have a degree, a sergeant's stripes or a specialist job. The thinking stuff goes first, so I'd want to be the person who manages the thinking stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the sergeant's exam next year after all, because leading people still matters. I'd do the criminology degree slowly over four or five years. I'd keep using every new tool as it comes. And Amara and I would buy the flat, because ten years of pay is ten years of mortgage paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit eager, honestly. It feels like something I can steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy the flat in this picture but not the fast one. Why the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years I can see my income for most of the loan. With two years, I can't see past 2030. It's the same flat on the same street, but the risk is totally different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older guys who refuse to touch a tablet, like my old tutor constable Pete. Pete is 51, he'd be 61 when it arrives, and he'll probably just retire. Honestly I worry more about the call handlers, who don't have that option.

say: Ten years is **a gift**, so nobody has an excuse not to plan.
Humans must make the **big calls**, and nobody gets thrown away.
think: At **37 and 40** he'd already have a degree and a senior role.
Thinking work goes first, so he wants to **manage the systems** doing it.
do: Sit the **sergeant's exam** next year after all.
Do the **criminology degree** slowly over four or five years.
Buy the **flat with Amara**, since ten years of pay is visible.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **eager** to steer it.
S4.quote: With ten years I can see my income for most of the loan. With two years, I can't see past 2030.
fieldNote: The **time window** decides his biggest money choice, the flat.
He worries for **call handlers** more than for himself.
He sees **leadership** as the part of policing that lasts.

steps.text: Sit the sergeant's exam next year
Do the criminology degree part time over five years
Buy the flat with Amara on a normal mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because my hands-on side buys me three years and that's not enough to retrain for anything. What would help is a deal, written now, that the force retrains officers into the roles that stay, like crisis work and checking the systems, with pay held while we train. And honestly, proper mental health services, because that problem is still there whatever the machines do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the public. People call the police at their worst moment. I don't think anyone in that moment wants to talk to a machine. We should ask them, not just the budget office.

headlineQuote: People call the police at their worst moment. I don't think anyone in that moment wants to talk to a machine.
portrait: Femi is a **27-year-old response officer** in the old docks area who loves crisis calls and hates paperwork.
He already uses **AI daily** to tidy his notes and sees most AI change as good for him.
As **union rep**, he keeps turning personal questions into fights about staffing and mental health services.
Fast AGI makes him **delay buying a flat**; ten years makes him buy it.
His plan is to move into **crisis negotiation** or checking how the force uses AI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three extra years for hands-on work isn't enough to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **written retraining deal** with pay held while officers train for lasting roles.
Proper **mental health services**, so officers stop doing that work.
